claim: Life history trade-offs are a pervasive attribute of life, and how organisms balance growth, reproduction, and survival governs much of their evolution.
source: Life history trade-offs are a pervasive attribute of life, and how organisms balance growth, reproduction, and survival governs much of their evolution (Stearns, 1989; Flatt, 2020; Bonsall et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three scholarly works (Stearns, 1989; Flatt, 2020; Bonsall et al., 2004) that establish this as accepted scientific knowledge.

claim: Simultaneous optimization of all traits is impossible as all individuals are limited by time, resources, or other factors.
source: Simultaneous optimization of all traits is impossible as all individuals are limited by time, resources, or other factors (van Noordwijk and de Jong, 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to van Noordwijk and de Jong, 1986, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Honey bee queens predictably and reversibly increase egg size in small colonies and decrease egg size in large colonies.
source: Here, we show in a series of experiments that queens predictably and reversibly increase egg size in small colonies and decrease egg size in large colonies, while their ovary size changes in the opposite direction.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the series of experiments described in the manuscript, including the repeated transfer experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Queen ovary size changes in the opposite direction to egg size (ovaries are smaller when producing larger eggs).
source: Here, we show in a series of experiments that queens predictably and reversibly increase egg size in small colonies and decrease egg size in large colonies, while their ovary size changes in the opposite direction.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2, showing ovary weight measurements.

claim: Egg-size plasticity is associated with quantitative changes of 290 ovarian proteins.
source: Egg-size plasticity is associated with quantitative changes of 290 ovarian proteins, most of which relate to energy metabolism, protein transport, and cytoskeleton.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data from LC-MS/MS analysis comparing ovaries from queens producing small versus large eggs.

claim: Most of the 290 differentially abundant proteins relate to energy metabolism, protein transport, and cytoskeleton.
source: Egg-size plasticity is associated with quantitative changes of 290 ovarian proteins, most of which relate to energy metabolism, protein transport, and cytoskeleton.
evidence: The claim is supported by GO enrichment and KEGG pathway analyses of the proteomic data.

claim: Rho1 has a major effect on egg size in honey bees.
source: subsequent RNAi-mediated gene knockdown confirmed that Rho1 has a major effect on egg size in honey bees.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RNAi knockdown experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: Sister queens housed in medium-sized colonies at the start of the first experiment produced a range of intermediate egg sizes with significant inter-individual differences.
source: Sister queens that were housed in medium-sized colonies at the start of our first experiment produced a range of intermediate egg sizes with significant inter-individual differences (ANOVA: F(10,219) = 31.5, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of experimental measurements.

claim: Over the course of the first week, egg sizes significantly increased while egg number did not differ significantly.
source: Over the course of the first week, egg sizes significantly increased (t = 5.8, df = 10, p<0.001) while egg number did not differ significantly (t = 0.7, df = 10, p<0.482).
evidence: The claim is supported by t-test statistical analysis of experimental measurements.

claim: The first and second egg size measurements were correlated, indicating consistent differences among queens.
source: The first and second measurements were correlated for egg size (RP = 0.80, n = 11, p=0.003), indicating consistent differences among queens, but not egg number (RP = 0.31, n = 11, p=0.350).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental measurements.

claim: After transfer from medium to small colonies, the egg size of all six queens increased significantly.
source: After transfer from medium to small colonies, the egg size of all six queens increased significantly (for each queen: F(1,38) = 23.7–153.3, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of experimental measurements for each individual queen.

claim: Egg size significantly decreased for all five queens that were transferred from medium to large colonies.
source: In contrast, egg size significantly decreased for all five queens that were transferred from medium to large colonies (F(1,38) = 8.9–53.2, all p<0.005).
evidence: The claim is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of experimental measurements for each individual queen.

claim: Egg-size adjustments were reversible because all three queens successfully transferred from large to small colonies significantly increased their egg sizes.
source: Our reciprocal transfers after the fourth week showed that egg-size adjustments were reversible because all three queens successfully transferred from large to small colonies significantly increased their egg sizes (F(1,38) = 143.8–1001.8, all p<0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of experimental measurements after reciprocal transfers.

claim: All five queens transferred from small to large colonies significantly decreased the size of their eggs.
source: all five queens transferred from small to large colonies significantly decreased the size of their eggs (F(1,38) = 123.0–699.4, all p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of experimental measurements after reciprocal transfers.

claim: There was a negative correlation between egg size and number in weeks 3-6, although this relation was only significant in weeks 3, 5, and 6.
source: While egg size and number were not significantly correlated while all queens were housed in medium colonies, there was a negative correlation between size and number in weeks 3–6, although this relation was only significant in week 3 (RP = –0.83, n = 11, p=0.002), week 5 (RP = –0.95, n = 8, p<0.001), and week 6 (RP = –0.90, n = 8, p=0.003).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental measurements.

claim: Queens in small colonies had significantly lighter ovaries than those in large colonies.
source: Queens in small colonies had significantly lighter ovaries than those in large colonies (F(1,8) = 10.2, p=0.013), while body size (F(1,8) = 0.3, p=0.596) and wet weight (F(1,8) = 0.8, p=0.402) did not differ (Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of experimental measurements and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Body size and wet weight did not differ between queens in small versus large colonies in the first experiment.
source: Queens in small colonies had significantly lighter ovaries than those in large colonies (F(1,8) = 10.2, p=0.013), while body size (F(1,8) = 0.3, p=0.596) and wet weight (F(1,8) = 0.8, p=0.402) did not differ (Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of experimental measurements and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The ovary weight difference between queens in small versus large colonies was confirmed in a second comparison.
source: These results were confirmed in a second comparison between queens that were simply housed in small versus large colonies after maturation (ovary: F(1,6) = 28.7, p=0.01; size: F(1,6) = 0.07, p=0.805; weight: F(1,6) = 0.3, p=0.627; Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of experimental measurements in a second independent experiment and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Similar-sized queens can differ in ovary weight and body weight.
source: A third comparison between queens housed in small versus large colonies indicated that similar-sized queens (F(1,10) = 0.1, p=0.748) can differ not only in ovary weight (F(1,10) = 18.5, p=0.002) but also in body weight (F(1,10) = 5.6, p=0.039; Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of experimental measurements in a third independent experiment and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No significant relationships between queen size and egg size were found for queens in small, medium, or large colonies.
source: Across these three experiments, no significant relationships between queen size and egg size were found for queens in small (RP = 0.11, n = 15, p=0.702), medium (RP = 0.21, n = 8, p=0.616), or large (RP = –0.22, n = 15, p=0.440) colonies.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis across three experiments.

claim: None of the four caged queens significantly changed egg size after a 2-week period of queen caging that prevented egg laying.
source: None of the four caged queens significantly changed her egg size (F(1,38) = 0.02–1.8, all p>0.1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of experimental measurements before and after caging.

claim: None of the four queens in an unmanipulated control group changed egg size during the same time period.
source: None of the four queens in an unmanipulated control group during the same time changed her egg size either (F(1,38) = 0.005–0.6, all p>0.4), and egg sizes were similar between the restricted and unrestricted groups overall (Figure 3, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of experimental measurements and shown in Figure 3.

claim: All three queens paired with a regular colony reduced the size of their eggs compared to their initial egg size.
source: All three queens paired with a regular colony reduced the size of their eggs compared to their initial egg size (Q1: F(3,76) = 34.5, p<0.001; Q2: F(3,76) = 42.5, p<0.001; Q3: F(3,76) = 14.6, p<0.001; post-hoc tests indicated significant differences only between measurements before and after manipulation; Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis with post-hoc tests of experimental measurements and shown in Figure 4.

claim: None of the three control queens significantly changed their egg size during the experimental period.
source: In contrast, none of the three control queens significantly changed their egg size during the experimental period (Q1: F(3,76) = 1.3, p=0.297; Q2: F(3,76) = 1.6, p=0.196; Q3: F(3,76) = 1.0, p=0.379; Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of experimental measurements and shown in Figure 4.

claim: A total of 2022 proteins were identified in the ovary proteome comparison.
source: To compare the ovary proteome of queens producing large eggs with that of queens producing small eggs, we identified a total of 2022 proteins and compared their relative abundance.
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS proteomic analysis data.

claim: Among the 290 proteins that exhibited significant quantitative differences, significantly more proteins were more abundant (275) than less abundant (15) in large-egg-producing ovaries compared to small-egg-producing ovaries.
source: Among the 290 proteins that exhibited significant quantitative differences, significantly more proteins were more abundant (275) than less abundant (15) in large-egg-producing ovaries compared to small-egg-producing ovaries (χ2 = 233.1, p<0.001; Figure 5A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by chi-square statistical analysis of proteomic data and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The proteins with increased abundance in large-egg-producing ovaries were significantly enriched in 10 biological process GO terms.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) analysis of the proteomic data showed that the proteins with increased abundance in large-egg-producing ovaries compared to small-egg-producing ovaries were significantly enriched in 10 biological process terms (Figure 5B and C, Supplementary file 3): 'protein localization' (p=0.00004), 'oxidation-reduction process' (p=0.00006), 'cytoskeleton organization' (p=0.00009), 'cellular homeostasis' (p=0.0003), 'protein processing' (p=0.006), 'nucleoside triphosphate metabolic process' (p=0.009), 'positive regulation of transport' (p=0.010), 'multicellular organism development' (p=0.011), 'oocyte construction' (p=0.046), and 'regulation of translational initiation' (p=0.048).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis of proteomic data and shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: No GO term was significantly enriched in the proteins that were less abundant in large-egg-producing ovaries than in small-egg-producing ovaries.
source: In contrast, no GO term was significantly enriched in the proteins that were less abundant than in small-egg-producing ovaries.
evidence: The claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis of proteomic data.

claim: KEGG analysis revealed an enrichment of seven key pathways in the proteins with increased abundance in large-egg-producing ovaries.
source: The KEGG analysis revealed an enrichment of seven key pathways in the proteins with increased abundance in large-egg-producing ovaries (Supplementary file 4), which included 'glycolysis/gluconeogenesis' (p=0.00002), 'citrate cycle (TCA cycle)' (p=0.00003), 'RNA transport' (p=0.0003), 'beta-alanine metabolism' (p=0.0005), 'protein processing in endoplasmic reticulum' (p=0.0005), 'proteasome' (p=0.0008), and 'oxidative phosphorylation' (p=0.004).
evidence: The claim is supported by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of proteomic data.

claim: No enrichment could be identified in the proteins that were less common in large-egg-producing ovaries compared to small-egg-producing ovaries in KEGG analysis.
source: Consistent with the GO analysis, no enrichment could be identified in the proteins that were less common in large-egg-producing ovaries compared to small-egg-producing ovaries.
evidence: The claim is supported by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of proteomic data.

claim: Of the 34 differentially expressed proteins associated with 'cytoskeleton organization,' 29 were connected by a protein–protein interaction (PPI) analysis.
source: Of the 34 differentially expressed proteins that were associated with 'cytoskeleton organization,' 29 were connected by a protein–protein interaction (PPI) analysis (Figure 6, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by PPI network analysis and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Five proteins had >10 connections to other proteins in the PPI network: Act5C (15), Rho1 (13), chic (12), Rac1 (11), and Tm2 (11).
source: This analysis pointed to five proteins with >10 connections to other proteins: Act5C (15), Rho1 (13), chic (12), Rac1 (11), and Tm2 (11).
evidence: The claim is supported by PPI network analysis data.

claim: Little Rho1 was expressed in the terminal filament but some expression was discernible in the germarium, concentrated in the cytocyst.
source: RNAscope in situ hybridization enabled a fine-scale characterization of Rho1 expression in the ovary, which was consistent with this hypothesis; little Rho1 was expressed in the terminal filament but some expression was discernible in the germarium, concentrated in the cytocyst (incipient oocyte).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization experimental data.

claim: Relatively strong expression of Rho1 was found in the growing oocytes of the vitellarium in contrast to nurse and follicle cells at that developmental stage.
source: Relative strong expression of Rho1 was found in the growing oocytes of the vitellarium in contrast to nurse and follicle cells at that developmental stage.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In mature oocytes, Rho1 expression was again low.
source: In mature oocytes, Rho1 expression was again low (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In the oocytes, Rho1 was mainly located near the lateral cell cortex, which may represent areas of longitudinal growth.
source: In the oocytes, Rho1 was mainly located near the lateral cell cortex, which may represent areas of longitudinal growth (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization experimental data shown in Figure 7B. The interpretation about longitudinal growth is speculative.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Rho1 resulted in an average of 35.1% reduced Rho1 expression compared to controls.
source: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Rho1 resulted in an average of 35.1% reduced Rho1 expression compared to controls (Figure 8A, Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Expression of Rho1 was on average 57.0% higher in control queens from small colonies that produce large eggs than queens from large colonies that produce small eggs.
source: Expression of Rho1 was also on average 57.0% higher in control queens from small colonies that produce large eggs than queens from large colonies that produce small eggs (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The knockdown of Rho1 consistently decreased egg sizes in all three queens in small colonies.
source: The knockdown of Rho1 consistently decreased egg sizes (Figure 8B, Figure 8—source data 2) in all three queens in small colonies (Q10: F(1,38) = 177.8, p<0.001; Q11: F(1,38) = 139.7, p<0.001; Q12: F(1,38) = 44.6, p<0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of experimental measurements after RNAi knockdown and shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The knockdown of Rho1 consistently decreased egg sizes in all three queens in large colonies.
source: The knockdown of Rho1 consistently decreased egg sizes (Figure 8B, Figure 8—source data 2) in all three queens in small colonies (Q10: F(1,38) = 177.8, p<0.001; Q11: F(1,38) = 139.7, p<0.001; Q12: F(1,38) = 44.6, p<0.001) and large colonies (Q4: F(1,38) = 63.7, p<0.001; Q5: F(1,38) = 42.8, p<0.001; Q6: F(1,38) = 28.1, p<0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of experimental measurements after RNAi knockdown and shown in Figure 8B.

claim: None of the six corresponding control queens exhibited significant egg-size changes.
source: while none of the six corresponding control queens exhibited significant egg-size changes (F(1,38) = 0.05–2.8, all p>0.1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of experimental measurements in control queens.

claim: Across individuals from all treatment groups, Rho1 expression at the end of the experiment correlated almost perfectly with the produced egg size.
source: Across individuals from all treatment groups, Rho1 expression at the end of the experiment correlated almost perfectly with the produced egg size (RP = 0.98, n = 12, p<0.001; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of Rho1 expression and egg size measurements.

claim: The correlation between Rho1 expression and egg size was confirmed in a second dataset of 12 queens that produced small and large eggs due to different colony sizes.
source: The correlation between Rho1 expression and egg size was confirmed in a second dataset of 12 queens that produced small and large eggs due to different colony sizes (RP = 0.90, n = 12, p<0.001; Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis in an independent dataset.

claim: Egg-size variation has been linked to parental or environmental conditions in numerous species.
source: Egg-size variation has been linked to parental or environmental conditions in numerous species (Dani and Kodandaramaiah, 2017; Fox and Czesak, 2000; Sánchez‐Tójar et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three scholarly works representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Egg size is typically increased under unpredictable or unfavorable conditions.
source: The direction of egg-size adjustments is consistent between solitary species and honey bees; egg size is typically increased under unpredictable or unfavorable conditions (Einum and Fleming, 2004; Rollinson and Hutchings, 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two scholarly works representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Egg size is positively correlated to maternal condition.
source: egg size is typically increased under unpredictable or unfavorable conditions (Einum and Fleming, 2004; Rollinson and Hutchings, 2013) and positively correlated to maternal condition (Fox and Czesak, 2000; Yu et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two scholarly works representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Larger eggs improve survival and offspring quality in honey bees.
source: Larger eggs improve survival and offspring quality in honey bees (Amiri et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two scholarly works.

claim: Small colonies may select for increased individual survival because each individual is proportionally more significant to the colony.
source: Small colonies may select for increased individual survival because each individual is proportionally more significant to the colony (Rueppell et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation and represents an inference about evolutionary selection.

claim: Large egg size in small colonies could also be directly related to less consistent brood care and overall colony-level resource availability.
source: but large egg size in small colonies could also be directly related to less consistent brood care and overall colony-level resource availability.
evidence: The claim is speculative, presenting an alternative hypothesis without direct supporting data.

claim: Older queens produce smaller eggs than young queens.
source: For example, older queens produce smaller eggs than young queens (Al-Lawati and Bienefeld, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a scholarly work.

claim: Queens in large colonies typically produce more eggs than queens in small colonies.
source: Queens in large colonies typically produce more eggs than queens in small colonies.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: Queens in large colonies have heavier ovaries, indicating a physiological adaptation to satisfy the egg-laying demand in large colonies.
source: Our finding that queens in large colonies have heavier ovaries indicates a physiological adaptation to satisfy the egg-laying demand in large colonies (Al-Khafaji et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the manuscript and a citation providing context.

claim: A simultaneous regulation of egg size and egg number in response to perceived colony size is more likely than a direct trade-off between these two variables.
source: Thus, a simultaneous regulation of egg size and egg number in response to perceived colony size is more likely than a direct trade-off between these two variables.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The perception of colony size by the queen is sufficient for her to adjust the size of her eggs.
source: Thus, our results suggest that the perception of colony size by the queen is sufficient for her to adjust the size of her eggs.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the colony extension experiment results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Direct physical contact among individuals can be excluded as the mechanism by which queens perceive colony size for egg-size adjustment.
source: We can exclude direct physical contact among individuals, which is used by worker honey bees to assess colony size (Smith et al., 2017), and thus we report a new modality by which honey bees perceive colony size.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental design using double-screened tunnels and supported by a citation about worker behavior.

claim: Multiple cues that travel through a double-screened tunnel could prompt the egg-size adjustment in queens, including sound, temperature, or pheromones and other semiochemicals.
source: Multiple cues that travel through a double-screened tunnel could prompt the egg-size adjustment in queens, including sound, temperature, or pheromones and other semiochemicals.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing possible mechanisms without direct evidence.

claim: Variation in parental care is intricately linked to the initial investment in eggs.
source: Broad comparisons find pronounced influences of social structure and behavior on egg size because variation in parental care is intricately linked to the initial investment in eggs (Dixit et al., 2017; Summers et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two scholarly works representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Queen- and worker-destined eggs differ in size even though they are presumably produced at almost the same time.
source: Adjustments may even be made instantaneously, as queen- and worker-destined eggs differ in size (Wei et al., 2019) even though they are presumably produced at almost the same time.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation and an inference about timing.

claim: The advantageous caste bias of larger eggs should select for paternal effects to increase egg size.
source: The advantageous caste bias of larger eggs (Al-Kahtani and Bienefeld, 2021) should select for paternal effects to increase egg size, in contrast to other polyandrous species in which males predominantly manipulate female fecundity (Hollis et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is an inference about evolutionary selection supported by citations.

claim: Plod, which controls egg length in Drosophila, is not among the differentially abundant proteins in honey bee ovaries.
source: Plod, which controls egg length in Drosophila (Lerner et al., 2013), is not among these proteins
evidence: The claim is based on proteomic data from the manuscript and a citation about Drosophila.

claim: Collagen IV is found more abundantly in large-egg-producing ovaries.
source: but collagen IV, which may influence egg size in Drosophila indirectly (Luo et al., 2021), is found more abundantly in large-egg-producing ovaries.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data from the manuscript and a citation about Drosophila.

claim: The anatomically smaller ovaries are physiologically more active in several key processes than the larger ovaries that produce smaller eggs.
source: Thus, the anatomically smaller ovaries are physiologically more active in several key processes than the larger ovaries that produce smaller eggs.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the proteomic data showing more abundant proteins in large-egg-producing (smaller) ovaries.

claim: Egg-size variation is not a simple increase of egg volume but reflects real differences in offspring provisioning.
source: These functional categories indicate that egg-size variation is not a simple increase of egg volume but reflects real differences in offspring provisioning, although the proteome of small and large eggs remains to be characterized (McDonough-Goldstein et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the GO and KEGG enrichment analyses, with a citation noting that egg proteome characterization remains to be done.

claim: Higher energy generation may be needed to produce more costly large eggs.
source: Higher energy generation may be needed to produce more costly large eggs (Wheeler, 1996)
evidence: The claim is an inference supported by a citation.

claim: The cytoskeleton and protein localization processes are key to loading the eggs with nutrients in polytrophic ovaries.
source: and the cytoskeleton and protein localization processes are key to loading the eggs with nutrients in polytrophic ovaries (Shimada et al., 2011; Wilson et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two scholarly works representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Cytoskeletal organization is the most likely regulatory mechanism for egg-size variation, while other processes are more likely involved in downstream effector functions.
source: Among all involved processes, we considered 'cytoskeletal organization' as the most likely regulatory mechanism, while other processes are more likely involved in downstream effector functions.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the functional analysis of proteomic data.

claim: Rho1 is a small, conserved GTPase with a likely role in egg-size regulation.
source: Thus, we identified Rho1 as a potential candidate because it was centrally located in the PPI network of proteins related to cytoskeletal organization that were abundant in large-egg-producing ovaries. Rho1 is a small, conserved GTPase with a likely role in egg-size regulation (Murphy and Montell, 1996) and thus also a plausible functional candidate.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a scholarly work.

claim: Rho1 generally plays an important role in cell morphogenesis by regulating the cytoskeleton.
source: Rho1 has multiple functions but generally plays an important role in cell morphogenesis by regulating the cytoskeleton (Hall, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Rho1 primarily has been implicated in actin regulation.
source: It primarily has been implicated in actin regulation (Hall, 1998), which is itself important for insect oogenesis (Sokolova et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two scholarly works representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Rho1 can also indirectly influence the microtubule network.
source: but can also indirectly influence the microtubule network (Pimm and Henty-Ridilla, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a scholarly work.

claim: The regulation of Rho1 activity is complex.
source: The regulation of Rho1 activity is complex (Denk-Lobnig and Martin, 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Multiple participating signaling pathways could transduce extracellular signals in the ovary into cytoskeletal reorganization of the eggs.
source: and multiple participating signaling pathways could transduce extracellular signals in the ovary into cytoskeletal reorganization of the eggs.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism without direct evidence.

claim: The observed spatio-temporal expression of Rho1 conforms well with the hypothesis that Rho1 influences egg growth in the vitellarium.
source: The observed spatio-temporal expression of Rho1 observed in our RNAscope experiment conforms well with the hypothesis that Rho1 influences egg growth in the vitellarium.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on RNAscope experimental data.

claim: Rho1 expression appeared to be focused in the cortex of oocytes close to the follicle cells, which mediate vitellogenin uptake.
source: Rho1 expression appeared to be focused in the cortex of oocytes close to the follicle cells, which mediate vitellogenin uptake (Fleig, 1995) and can influence egg size (Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on RNAscope experimental data and supported by citations about follicle cell function.

claim: Vitellogenesis is the period of rapid egg growth, and small differences during this time may cause significant differences in the size of the mature egg.
source: Vitellogenesis is the period of rapid egg growth, and small differences during this time may cause significant differences in the size of the mature egg.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about insect oogenesis and inference.

claim: Resulting eggs from Rho1 knockdown only differed in size, suggesting that the knockdown of Rho1 does not cause pathological effects.
source: Resulting eggs only differed in size, suggesting that the knockdown of Rho1 does not cause pathological effects.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on observations of eggs after RNAi treatment.

claim: The tight correlation between egg size and Rho1 expression strengthens the interpretation that social conditions, inter-individual differences, and RNAi manipulation all act through Rho1 in a comparable manner to influence egg size.
source: The almost perfect correlation between Rho1 expression and egg size of queens across two different colony sizes and RNAi treatment groups strengthens the interpretation that social conditions, inter-individual differences, and RNAi manipulation all act through Rho1 in a comparable manner to influence egg size.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on correlation analysis across multiple experimental conditions.

claim: Honey bee queens adjust their egg size depending on whether a worker- or queen-destined egg is laid.
source: Honey bee queens also adjust their egg size depending on whether a worker- or queen-destined egg is laid (Wei et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a scholarly work.

claim: Egg size influences the probability that an egg is raised into a future queen.
source: and egg size influences the probability that an egg is raised into a future queen (Al-Kahtani and Bienefeld, 2021) and her reproductive quality (Wei et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scholarly works.

claim: Egg size influences the reproductive quality of future queens.
source: and egg size influences the probability that an egg is raised into a future queen (Al-Kahtani and Bienefeld, 2021) and her reproductive quality (Wei et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scholarly works.

claim: The comparative results of the ovary proteome suggest that larger eggs are indeed of superior quality.
source: Our comparative results of the ovary proteome suggest that larger eggs are indeed of superior quality, but a comparison of the actual egg content remains to be performed to substantiate this argument.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on proteomic data, with acknowledgment that direct egg content comparison is needed.

claim: Rho1 may become an important indicator of stress and maternal quality in ongoing efforts to sustain honey bee health.
source: If so, Rho1 may become an important indicator of stress (Amiri et al., 2020) and maternal quality (Yu et al., 2022) in the ongoing efforts to sustain honey bee health.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a potential application with citations for context.

claim: Social insect queens may not be resource-limited despite their very high reproductive effort.
source: As such, social insect queens may not be resource-limited despite their very high reproductive effort (Schrempf et al., 2017).

claim: Honey bee queens display plasticity in egg size that is consistent with patterns in solitary species and corresponds to an adaptive investment hypothesis.
